before: Many things please and nourish, but lordship belongs only to God, who possesses life incorruptibly and imperishably. I saw an inn, where a traveler stayed; he took many things from there without owning any: a bed, a table, vessels, a plate, and other various utensils. No one has ever used them for self-sufficiency, but rather someone comes, becomes greedy, acts impetuously, plunders the inn, and seeks what belongs to others as if it were his own.

Such is our life, brothers, and if anything of what has been said is more temporary. I marvel at those who say, 'my place' or 'my house,' so that they in vain claim ownership of what does not belong to them, and they embrace foreign things with three deceptive elements. Just as the masks of those performing wonders belong to no one in particular, but all the actors in the plays wear them, so others clothe themselves with the earth and its materials from others as if they were clothing.

Tell me, is there anything more powerful than a kingdom? Yet search the kingdoms; seek royal robes, and you will find them sufficient, though they have clothed many kings. Likewise, the crowns, the purple robes, and the belts—all are an unstable inheritance, a common use passing from those traveling to those staying.

What of the value of the possessor—the tent, the silver chariot, the golden reed? The possessor does not always have these, nor always the same, except for a short time for each. Just as the bed of the journey receives different bodies at different times, so the symbols of rulers change for those using them.

From this, the apostle cried out many instructive voices regarding this mindset: he presents the form of this world, namely, 'as having nothing and possessing all' (1 Tim 6:7), and 'those using as if not using' (1 Cor 7:31). For all these tend toward one aim: that it was fitting for us to live as sojourners, remembering the covenant of the exodus.

And so that you may learn accurately that you are subject to laws and masterly canons, according to which it is fitting for you to live accurately, first understand from yourself that both your body and your soul are subject everywhere to the commands of virtue, and you are not even master of yourself; rather, it is fitting for you to manage both word and deed and all...

The movement of your life. You received a body from the Creator, composed of many parts and being managed by five senses for the needs of life. But even these are not free and autonomous, but each is a slave to laws.

And first, the eye hears; look at nature and behold what is beautiful to see: the sun, lighting the whole inhabited world; the moon, illuminating the dark and gloomy night; the other stars, which are not many, nor sufficient for us, providing the light from themselves, except for the beauty they reflect. Behold the earth, adorned with all kinds of plants and herbs; the sea lying flat like a level plain, when it is in a pure calm. To these and such things you have been accustomed to seeing; but the other sights, as many as introduce harm to the soul through sight, flee from them and run away, and impose a covering upon yourself so that you may not see. For it is better to darken the sense when it holds the cause of the works of darkness. For this reason, the Lord said to us yesterday through Matthew: 'Every man who looks at a woman to lust after her has already committed adultery with her in his heart' (Matthew 5:28); and it is better to cut it off when it looks disordered and with injury.

Hearing also has prohibitive commands against bad listening. For it is necessary that when it hears of certain good things, it should be uplifted and send the sense to the soul through the beneficial words. But if a companion of wickedness, a plague and a corruption, approaches it, it must repel the filth of sin like a venomous beast.

Let the tongue also be temperate with the mouth; let it speak the righteous things; and let it abstain from the forbidden: reviling, slandering, unjust accusation, backbiting against brothers, and blasphemy against God. But let it utter whatever is well-spoken, whatever is pious, whatever has the counsel of good deeds; and let every man say the things of the Psalmist: 'I said: I will guard my ways, lest I sin with my tongue' (Psalm 119:11); and that, 'Their tongues were a stumbling block' (Psalm 57:4); and that, 'What boasts a strong man in wickedness, the power of lawlessness?' (Psalm 73:4). All the day your tongue reckoned injustice; you made a snare like a sharpened razor.
Let the taste be of those things which benefit the stomach. Let the nose also be temperate, not always smelling luxury, nor the vapors of expensive myrrh.

before: You were initiated by the more prominent apostles into the truth that the Father has a genuine, beloved Son. I show myself to you so that you may be able to bear the burden. And the Son stood by my side, so that you might know his honor by the relation of place. At that time, many were scandalized that God had clothed himself in flesh on earth; but see him now in the heights, with me, bearing the form of man in the heavenly and hyper-heavenly realms, as a confirmation of the completed economy. Do not be crushed or grow limp by being overwhelmed by this.

Looking at the athlete, do not be afraid of the contest. Do not despise the body, treating it as an earthly bond, a fragile house, or a corrupt vessel of a potter. Ascend toward the end here in freedom, for the crown of manliness is ready for you. Transfer from the earth to heaven. Leave the body to the scavengers like food for dogs. Leave behind a raging people and come to the dance of angels.

After this resolve, God appeared to the patient one, so that he might not suffer something cowardly, and might release much eagerness through the greatness of fear. Therefore, God neither sent him an angel as a helper, as he later did for the apostles in prison (Acts 12:5), nor any ministerial and fellow-servant power, but he manifested himself. For it was then the firstfruits of the testimony, and it was necessary for the first work to be completed, so that those following, being built up as witnesses, might receive a strong foundation of zeal and not become imitators of cowardice, which is exactly what happens in common wars. For one soldier, a champion, providing the glorious part of the work, having conquered and having emboldened all his own, strikes down the opponents; yet, having suffered a slight injury, he immediately collapses and fills the souls of his kinsmen with cowardice, and flight becomes a habit. For this reason, God appeared from heaven.

But he who was worthy of the great vision did not hold in silence what he saw, but immediately cried out: 'Behold, I see the heavens opened and the Son of Man standing at the right hand of God!' (Rev 4:1). For he thought that the revealing of the vision would draw the unbelievers into agreement. But those making the spoken word a starting point for greater wrath and madness, attempting to block...

They held their ears against the word as if it were blasphemy, immediately ready for death. Dragging the Christ-bearing man outside the city, bearing his endurance as the Lord bore the cross, they return evil for evil and justify murder with murder, and with stones they bind the one who serves the cornerstone.

Standing him on a certain level field, that long body and high trophy of the martyrs, the mob of blood and wrath surrounded him, and imitating the sling used in wars, they threw stones at the servant of the cornerstone, and every Hebrew hand enacted the murder; the aim was for those leaving that the martyr stood in the middle like a target for an archer.

As the body was shattered from every side and smeared with blood, it rushed toward the upright position; it leaned and threatened to fall like a tall plane tree being worked on by many carpenters; but it did not suffer an improper fall according to the many. For it was not cast headlong, nor was it thrown on its side, nor was the form reclined upon its back, but having set its knees in the proper form of one praying, it descended, hastening with the soul through prayer the separation from the flesh and crying out to the visible Lord: 'Lord Jesus Christ, receive my spirit.'

For he was hastening as if to some migration, as if from a foreign land to a fatherland, as if to a bright city from a desert and smoky land. And he added to his petition the prayer for those throwing stones. For those blessing and those stoning were saving, and those murdering were making alive, and those separating from the clay were sending to the kingdom.

Let us therefore consider also the word of the prayer, regarding toward what end it carries 'Lord, do not hold their sin against them' (Luke 23:34). For it is not, as some wickedly thinking men suppose, that the sin of the enemies becomes unpunished and unaccountable. For this was clearly to stand against God's decree and to restore the judgment and law of the righteous, having completed what was due to the murderers.
But what does he say? 'Lord, do not hold their sin against them,' that is: Give the fear of compunction, lead to repentance those now having dared,

before: A participant in your virtue, Tarso, who through a different mode of punishment, but with a single purpose of piety, analyzed himself with you toward Christ. Paul the lawgiver, the loud-voiced trumpet of the gospel, who formerly was a bitter enemy of Christians, but finally a strong advocate for the church, was more recently reached by the apostles through grace; and in time he was second among the disciples of Christ, but equal according to the proven virtue, so that I may say nothing more than to exceed the twelve in redness. He was a zealous follower of Moses, if anyone else was, a wall of the law, a tower of the Old Testament, enduring and unshakeable; and until he held his purpose unchangeable, there was a great danger to those speaking of Christ, and he fled everywhere from our [people]. Truly, according to the prophecy of Jacob (Gen 49:10), a wolf snatched the Benjamin, tearing the lambs of the New Testament and scattering the flocks.

Because he also performed the drama according to Saint Stephen, and having his hands still stained with blood, he ran toward Damascus, seeking to join persecution to persecution and murder to murder, and to uproot Christianity, the first blooming nature. Our God saw well what he had done, that the strong enemy might become a noble friend; and having suddenly surrounded him with light, He strikes him with astonishment and changes him toward humility, making him stand in the road through fear, and having brought to sobriety the eyes that were looking with fiery and angry temper through the darkness. And He punishes him not in silence, but also added a word to the deed, saying that written thing: 'Saul, Saul, why do you persecute me? It is hard for you to kick against the pricks' (Acts 26:14). For it was not as if he himself needed a discussion, since the words of the facts were sufficient, but so that he might have an occasion within to ask and to learn that he who was thought to be dead and to be Christ lives, and appears from the heavens, and thus defends those who are grieving from authority. Nothing is more like the words themselves to explain to us the hunt of the Hebrew wolf.
And Saul, still breathing threats and murder, the word describes to me a man whose mind is being shattered by the [pressure]...

While the mixed nature of the event was still being perceived through the whistling of the stones, seeing a wind and a wild thing as if it were the murderer, the symbols were being saved in the beginning of the patriarch's prophecy. For he, since he was about to die, having surrounded his children from every side, foretold by the Spirit at the bedside.

Thus, while blessing Judah, he was speaking in one way, but allegorically he praised the Christ coming from him. Furthermore, having prophesied to all the things to come, he came last upon Benjamin, who was also more recent in time; and at times he spoke toward the son, but in reality he signified Paul, as we know, descending from that tribe. 'Benjamin is a wolf; in the morning he shall snatch, and in the evening he shall deliver prey' (Gen 49:27).

Let us investigate what is said. Is it certainly this: that after having eaten the first things—that is, having pursued, having murdered, having shed blood, having scattered the church like a flock—he became last a shepherd and a good pastor, having laid aside the persecutor and having put on the apostle, distributing to all as food the Word and having established this holy table for us?

For the power of the Lord is such, disarming the fury and the impious thoughts of those standing in opposition, and approaching gracefully and subduing, working to make sheep by day instead of beasts that tear. For every one who fights for piety is good, even if he becomes second or third to those who competed before; yet he is not worthy of such a marvel as the first. The second, being stirred by zeal for the one who preceded, was thus drawn toward diligence; but he who uses no one as a guide, yet having become a discoverer of the good, appropriately receives the vote of the first.

Great indeed is the man's readiness, therefore great is the honor; and immortal is the memory, which neither oblivion covered nor time dimmed, but generation after generation, inheriting the stories, we priests, people, children, men, and women, celebrate this feast without fail. But the history itself should also be observed, so that, having become acquainted with the facts of the matters, we might more marvel at the man.

First among those who serve according to Christ was Stephen, esteemed by grace, a vessel filled with the Spirit, confirming daily those in the household and those wandering toward the straight path. And because he had a more intense teaching, he more than the other apostles loosed the enemies and, before them, first made the devil hostile. For he sets his eyes like fire and looks fiercely at those who are more steadfast in piety. Thus the race of Alexandrians raised up a sharp-edged system against him for a stand. In any case, you have heard of the men of the city, how they are both fervent and boiling upon everything they might readily rush toward. And when the crowd saw those rushing toward him, it had almost been possible to set the present situation aside; however, he found a resourceful, well-composed, and gentle word. For there is no medicine of such a kind for the healing of temper and agitation, such as a pleasant and well-fitted exhortation.

And 'tell me,' he says, 'the cause of the hatred, instead of why you stretch out your hands and are manifest as if about to strike.' The ray of the sun provides a covering for the vegetable that is withering, yet the shadow, failing to provide continuous protection, dries it up. Then, as if struggling to wake up to what is happening, it [the person] reproaches and blames. If one so passionately grieves over a withered vegetable, would God not be moved by a city approaching such danger? Learn, then, you harsh and unmerciful ones, the goodness of Him who created us, and do not become bitter and heavy-handed judges among fellow slaves, until He who reveals the secrets of hearts arrives to distribute the state of the expected life to each according to their lot by His sovereign authority. Do not issue your decisions in secret, so that you may not be subjected to the same, and walk as if pierced by the words of your own people as if they were sharp. For it seems to me that even the Gospel forewarning of this serves as a safeguard, saying: 'Do not judge, so that you may not be judged' (Matthew 7:1). For it does not cast out judgment and good-knowledge, but names the harshest condemnation 'judgment.' Therefore, if you wish, make the scale light, if you do not want to be dragged down by the condemning tablet and your own deeds when our life is being weighed in the balance of God's judgment.

Being surrounded by a body and living in the flesh, do not ever reject life from medical treatment. For even if you live for a long time in both well-being and health, you will not continue to be without sickness as if there were no need for the care of the healer. And having a soul inclined toward earthly things, whenever it becomes filled with the efforts of the body, do not reject mercy, so that you may not be deprived of forgiveness when you become in need of it. If someone is a priest and has been granted to lead the people, let him see the falls of those under his care with sympathy, knowing that even if the order of life differs from the many, it has not hindered the nature of those being shepherded, and that he, sharing in it, may perhaps one day share in transgression. Moses, knowing these things—for he was a man and knew human nature—commanded the calf to be used by the priest, because he was entirely a sinner and in need of cleansing and many things. What the fleshly calf was then, this is now the bodiless [sin].

before: Stories are given to those who honor the struggles. As if someone were a devoted friend of the excellent martyrs, and set his care upon celebrating their sufferings, not a single day of the year would pass unobserved. For the exploits of brave men possess a glory superior to the solar cycle.

Because the one who opposes the good has attacked the Christian faith fiercely, and sought to destroy all through his schemes and calamities, and to occupy himself vainly with the tasks of the flesh, God, having anointed a multitude of excellent men with commands and trained them for endurance and strength, set them against the shameless and the enemy of humanity.. These, moreover, faced a new kind of struggle. For they did not prevail by striking or smashing, but they excelled   by suffering and by being slaughtered.

And what kind of power would you say, listener, is this of war? And what kind of success is this: to be twisted and flogged, and to have one's life destroyed through fire or sword or the cruelty of prisons? But learn how the wars for piety are won in a different way than other wars. For some have excellence in killing, but others achieve victory without bloodshed through suffering and falling. And the boldness of the righteous carries out missions against the world. And the enemy was caught off guard by the adversaries, whether he fell or intended to. For however many he slaughtered as martyrs, so many helpers of men he prepared.

And in every kind of action, this is found in suffering; therefore, where they think they are obstructing piety, they actually prepare its increase. For the wise God stands against the purposes of the fool and the thoughtless. And we find this throughout the events of every time: the exposition of Moses and the conduct of Joseph. Immediately in the beginning, the second man murdered Abel (Gen 4:8), so that he might cut off the seed of the pious, yet it became fruitful. For from then on, man-slayers are intensely hated, which is why Cain was cursed by God (Gen 4:15). The matter of Christ, that the Satan worked in the Jews so that they might crucify him (Matt 27), is the same. The same thing has happened to the martyrs, whom many despise, trivializing their [life/existence] through their own folly...
A reproach. Is he not a man? Was not the body spent? Is not their memory contained in a few remains and these things? Especially Greeks and Euomians say these things; let us speak to both.

We do not worship martyrs, but honor them as genuine worshippers of God; we do not revere men, but marvel at those who, in the time of trials, have reverently served God well. We place them in beautiful shrines and raise up houses of their rest with magnificent constructions, so that we may emulate the honors of those who well finished their course; and we do not show our zeal for them for pay, but we enjoy their protection toward God.

For our prayer is not sufficient to move God in the time of necessity or misfortune, for our plea is not a persuasion, but a remembrance of sins; therefore we fly to the fellow-servants who are loved by the Lord, so that they might heal our defects through their own achievements. What then is the charge, that while honoring martyrs we ourselves strive to please God? What accusation is there in flying to protectors? Let us examine also these things, if the accuser cleanses the charge. And how [can it be said], that you do not honor myriads of dead men, but worship them as gods?

Did you not, through your folly, deify Demeter and Kore, and yet you honor two women with temples and these sacrifices and with all kinds of worships and healings? Are not the mysteries at Eleusis the essence of your religion, and the Attic people and all Greece flowing together to complete a vanity? Is not the dark descent there, and the solemn gatherings of the hierophant toward the altar, only from woman to woman? Do not the torches go out, and the large and countless people think their salvation to be the things done in the darkness by the two?

Do I say that you worship Dionysus the Theban as a god? For I say, know your fatherland, so that you may know the man: a man, a grape-grower and a vintner, a village leader, a people drawing together and acting shamefully through drunkenness, doing those things which incite the dissolute youths to unchastity, while they drink with the old Silenus and the satyrs who love revelry.

Likewise, for Elijah, the one who guided this prophet with the flaming horses and the fiery chariot, living in another kind of life and having departed from men to the place he received, he left a symbol sufficient of his own power, even the mantle. Yet what was the value of that thing? For it was nothing other than a dead and trivial skin from old age. However, even the Jordan itself yielded to it, and the water was split and stood divided, just as the old [Jordan] was before Jesus, who was a type of what was to come (2 Kings 2:11).

The Theban [Elisha] also was present, and he received the garment of the philosopher as a disciple, making the crossing of the river secure, honoring the philanthropy of God and the garments of the saints as if they were endowed with soul. And so that it might be clearly shown that the miracle concerning the river did not happen because of the cause of the water being struck, but because of the honor of the one inhabited and taken up, Elisha struck the water, and the water flowed normally, nothing new having suffered. And since, having failed, he cried out: 'Where is the God of Elijah?' (2 Kings 2:14), and having cried out a second time, he sat down, immediately the river split the stream, showing the dry land, and the prophet, having trodden, arrived at the other side.

And Joseph, after Jacob had died, not loving him as a father so privately, but honoring him as a common patriarch of the nation, with that much-celebrated service, led the remains out of Egypt, so as to allow Moses, after the writing of the world's genesis and the rest of the history, to give this also as a narrative of life. And Joseph again was present with the Israelite departing from the eyes, as one might say, stolen from Pharaoh, and the body was everywhere present with the people, and he led it with care as a good and evil-averting safeguard for the sixty myriads.

And they had such reverence regarding the ark of the forefather, as regarding the holy ark which bore the law of God. Therefore also David, entreating God to be propitious and favorable to the people, and exhausting him with myriads of supplications, so that having stilled the continuous and recurring plague of misfortunes, he might again govern Jerusalem with good foresight as before, thus says: 'O Shepherd of Israel, pay attention, O Leader of Joseph like a sheep' (Ps 80:2). For he is appeased by the names of the beloved and friends, and most gracefully handles the entreaty of the transgressing multitude of sins, as if concealing and covering them with the titles of the holy fathers.

This is told to our mind by the word concerning the saving of Sodom (Gen 18-19). For Abraham, entreating the Sodomites, when God, after foretelling, brought the punishment upon them as they were displeased, the sparing of the righteous being worthy to save the whole people. For beginning from the fifty toward the ten, he concluded, and God immediately granted the entreaty, as if weighing on some scale and weights, opposing the value of the ten righteous against the myriads of sinners.

In order that it might be shown more abundantly to us all, that even one righteous person is a precious thing and a friend to God, since the tenth failed to be a number and the multitude of the holy was found suffering from the smallness of the sinners, and it was necessary for the law-breakers to receive the penalty of audacity; Lot is violently driven from the condemned places and is saved entirely into the old age of his own righteousness, having received all his household from God (Gen 19). Therefore, a righteous person is a great possession: first, a benefit to himself; second, a lasting treasure to the rest of his race, unknown to sight and always accompanying them, silent and instructing others by his deeds; lying of old and living by his good repute. Good for the children.

before: A speculator and a lover of money. He is nourished by water and pulse, even if formerly he was full of luxury and set a Sybaritic table. Separated from his usual marriage-bed, he does not delight children; he understands doctors both by night and by day, and for the sake of beloved profit, he hastens toward health with many wages. Such is the sick man of the body.

But he who is badly disposed regarding the soul, having surrounded the incorporeal [soul] with [physical] ailments, and feigning confession and showing weakness, leaves [it] to be devoured and torn apart by the passion, so that it might be spread out over the whole mass? But be temperate, know yourself: you have grieved God, having insulted your Creator, who has authority over this present life and is Lord and Judge of the life to come. It is therefore worthy to observe the response, how in brevity and conciseness he most accurately revealed the mind in a few words, beginning from the lower things and leading the mind upward toward the high things step by step.

The soul of such a person, having tasted some water of Lethe, completely forgets who she is and with whom she is joined, and that she will one day be released from this union and, having been resurrected, will dwell again with the body. But when the time of the necessary and appointed command comes, which severs her from the fellowship with the body, a calculation of what has been lived enters, and a useless repentance occurs after the need has arisen. For regret is only a sorrow when the one reconsidering still has the power to correct; but when the activity of the one doing right has been taken away, sorrow is worthless and the change of mind is vain.

There was once a man named Lazarus (Luke 16:20). The word does not describe him as a mere poor man, but as one deprived of the necessities of spending and need, and also being tormented by painful sickness and having a body broken, homeless, unsupported, untreated, thrown at the gate of the rich. And with great care in the narration, he brings the misfortunes of the poor to a tragic climax, so as to expose the hardness of the one who does not show mercy. For he who suffers nothing from hunger or disease is an irrational beast, pitiless or sympathetic, a form badly shaped into a human, falsely pretending nature by his intention; rather, he is even more unsympathetic than the beasts themselves; for even pigs, when one is being slaughtered, are drawn to a certain sad sensation and trouble the butcher with their blood; but oxen stand by such a slaughter, empathizing with a sound, signaling the pain. And herds of sheep, when one of the flock falls into the clutches of wild beasts, fall into a state where the one held is being sought, and some mournful sound fills the air, seeking its kind and companion. But a human, the rational animal, who is day-by-day being educated in goodness according to the likeness of God, cares so little...

Oh, the relatives in the painful circumstances of misfortunes! Thus lay the much-painful and blessed poor man, not having feet, for he would have fled the insolent and proud one, having changed to another place; instead of the murderous gate, being deprived of hands by the closed hands of the poor, and not even having a palm to stretch out for a request, being obstructed by those very organs of the voice and producing a certain hoarse and rough sound of the sternum, simply maimed in all his limbs, leaving behind a wicked disease, a pitiful example of human weakness.

If you zeal for God as having been created according to an image, imitate the archetype yourselves; O Christians, the Philanthropic name, zeal for the love of Christ, and turn toward the wealth of his philanthropy. For, intending to appear to men through a man, he preordained John, the preacher of repentance (Luke 3:3), the introducer of regret, and all before John as teachers of turning, the prophets. Then also he himself, having appeared after a little time, cries with his own voice personally: 'Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened, and I will give you rest (Matt 11:28).'

How did he respond when persuaded by the call? He gave a remission of sins without cost, and a release from those who grieve that is uncalculated and brief. The Word sanctified, the Spirit sealed; the old man was buried by the water, the new man was born rising by grace.

What follows? A man becomes his own instead of an alien, a son instead of a stranger, a mystic out of the profane, a holy one out of the ungodly. Therefore, having been enriched by such magnificent and unsurpassed gifts, if one, sinning against the ambitious and good benefactor, were not immediately mindful of the word before you difficult and negligent judges, he would certainly be driven to destruction, being cut off from this life and being punished there.

But since another is the Lord of the verdict, who makes mercy into thousands and myriads and does not wish the death of the sinner, but awaits the return, even so those who insulted the former grace were not punished; rather, a second mercy follows the first, and forgiveness is joined with amnesty. A tear falling is equal to the washing, and a groan over toil brings back the grace that had withdrawn a little.

If you do not believe the word, ask Peter, sitting in the house of the high priest, and he will tell you how, bitterly mourning the lapse of his denial, he was cleansed, and he did not dissolve into Simon, but Peter remained the apostle.

I myself think that even Judas Iscariot, if he had quickly become his own executioner, judging his sin unpardonably and falling down to ask mercy, would not have missed the mercies that overflow throughout the inhabited world. The proof of this word is all the Hebrews who, after the cross, believed, washing their souls and their hands together in the washing. If those who crucified were shown mercy, how could the betrayer not have escaped the amnesty?

For, intending to appear to men through a man, he preordained John, the preacher of repentance (Luke 3:3), the introducer of regret, and all before John as teachers of turning, the prophets. What follows? A man becomes his own instead of an alien, a son instead of a stranger, a mystic out of the profane, a holy one out of the ungodly. For he proclaimed with word what these hold and rule with works. When they appear clothed, they are seen like walls painted by passers-by. Even children stand around them, laughing at one another and pointing to the writing on the garments; and they walk past, not stopping for long.

There are lions and leopards, bears and bulls and dogs; woods and rocks, and men beast-slayers, and all the skill of painting imitating nature. For it was necessary not only their walls, as it seems, and their houses to be decorated, but already also their tunics and the clothes upon them.

As for those who are more pious than the wealthy ones, having reviewed the Gospel history, they handed it over to the weavers; I say the Christ our Lord meeting with the disciples, each miracle as the narrative has it: the wedding in Galilee and the water; the paralytic carrying the bed on his shoulders (Mark 2:1-12); the blind man being healed with mud (Matthew 8:1-4); the woman bleeding being taken by the edge of the garment (Luke 8:43); the sinful woman falling at the feet of Jesus (Luke 7:36-50); Lazarus returning to life from the tomb (John 11:1-44).

And doing these things, they think they are being pious and putting on garments graced by God. But if they accept counsel, let them, having sold those things, honor the living images of God. Do not paint Christ; for it is enough for Him the one part of the incarnation, humility, which He freely received through us, but carry the incorporeal Word mentally upon your soul. Do not have the paralytic on your garments, but seek the one lying sick. Do not constantly recount the woman bleeding, but have mercy on the grieving widow. Do not look carefully at the sinful woman prostrating herself before the Lord, but let the tear flow thick, being crushed by his own faults. Do not sketch Lazarus being raised from the dead, but prepare a good defense for your own resurrection. Do not carry the blind man on your clothing, but the living one deprived of sight.

Encourage with acts of goodness. Do not paint the remains of the dead in a flattering way, but nourish those who hunger. Do not carry the water-skins upon the garments, which He filled in Cana of Galilee (John 2:7), but give drink to the thirsty.

Regarding these things, the proud clothing of the rich man benefited us, and not only that, but also what follows. For luxury was added to the purple and the fine linen daily and brilliantly; yet, in both respects, it is of one single mind: to be adorned by useless vanity in delicacies, and to serve the palate and the throat with pleasant sensations.

Luxury, therefore, is a thing hostile to a virtuous life, signifying emptiness and dissipation, excessive enjoyment and a slave-like habit. And while the thing appears to be one, when examined in parts and accused, its composition consists of a diverse, greater, and manifold evil. For luxury could not exist unless increased by many materials. But as for accumulating the materials of wealth, one might without sin fail to lose nothing, unless, perhaps, according to the small measure, as with Job (Job 1:10), it should happen to one both to prosper abundantly and to live strictly according to justice.

Therefore, it is necessary for one living in luxury, first, to have a costly house, decorated with votes, stones, and gold according to the patterns, and to have it conveniently suited to the changes of the seasons of the year. For warmth is sought; the winter is wretched and turned away from the midday sun, having risen toward the North, while the summer is [warm], so that it may be breathed upon by thin and cold northern breezes. After this, there is the need for costly clothing for the beds, the couches, the mattresses, and the doors that are about to be clothed. For everything, even the inanimate things, is carefully clothed by those, as the wretched are stripped of their belongings.

Add to these also and consider the silver in the vessels, the gold, the expensive purchase of birds from Phasais, and the wine of the Phoenician, which the vines of Tyre pour out much and precious to the rich; and all the preparation of the rest of enjoyment, which those using it have carefully named. For luxury, increasing daily toward the more curious, already pours out the scents from India upon the faces, and more so, the perfumers serve the cooks rather than the physicians.

And when he arrives at the allotted place, hearing, 'Render the account of your stewardship; show how you heard the commandments, how you dealt with fellow-slaves, either kindly and philanthropically or, on the contrary, greedily and tyrannically, striking, beating, and depriving them of the grain-measure of alms.'

If he is able to make the master appeased by proving himself a good servant, it would be well for him; but if on the contrary, there are no longer whips and rods there, nor dark mills and iron pedals, but unquenchable fire and eternal darkness never illuminated by light, and the gnashing of teeth, which the gospel has clearly revealed to us (Matt 25:30).

Therefore, if he never casts out from here as if they were strangers, let him waste the world and let pleasure remain unhindered according to every sense. But if these things will be accomplished, even if we do not enjoy them for long, let us fear, brothers, the transfer from this place, and let us live in the time of sojourning as the Lord commanded; let us not be carried away as debtors, but let us walk free, being led by a good conscience, carrying the books of the life's citizenship unsearchably.

That rich man was a bad steward of this life, whose land was fruitful, because regarding the abundance of fruits, man did not counsel anything good, but opening the desire of the stomach and the wide and insatiable bellies of greed, he allotted everything to his own enjoyment, saying, 'I will pull down my barns and build greater, and I will say to my soul: You have many good things laid up, rest, eat, drink, rejoice' (Luke 12:19-20). And while he was speaking, the one taking him arrived. A terrible fellow-slave came to snatch him away from the stewardship; and what is the profit of a love-of-money plan?

And these things were written vividly for our instruction. But what is the experience of life? Not every single day do these things cry out through works; I showed us the one healthy in the middle of the day becoming dead before the onset of evening; and the one strengthening himself in the evening, not grasping the morning ray; and another perishing in the midst of eating and living. Who then is so foolish, as not to realize that every day another [comes] of this [place]...

Are we being moved from our stewardship? But the good and faithful steward, having trusted in his own management, has a will such as Paul had. For he, when the Lord was not hurrying, hastened to him and desired the dismissal and was willing to relinquish the stewardship, saying in one way: 'Wretched am I a man, who will rescue me from this body of death?' (Rom 7:24) and again: 'For to me it is good to be dissolved and to be with Christ' (Phil 1:23). But the earthly man, whose mindset is truly kin to the oxen, laments such things helplessly at the transition, like this man in the parable: 'What shall I do, since my lord is taking the stewardship from me? I am not able to dig, and I am ashamed to beg' (Luke 12:48).

His grief is that of the idle and the lover of pleasure. For to wail at the departure is a reproach of having been added to the estate and of lamenting the passionate enjoyments of the flesh, while the inability toward the work of an idle life and a fallen state is an accusation. For if he had had a habit of love for labor, he would not have feared digging.

If we take the parable allegorically toward the spiritual, after this transition, there is neither working nor having time for increase. And because of this, let no one say: 'I am not able to dig.' For even if he is able, no one forgives. This life holds the agriculture of the commandments, while the one coming holds the enjoyment. So if you worked nothing here, the vines remained, and you care excessively about the spade; nor will you benefit yourself by having time.

And when he arrives at the allotted place, hearing, 'Render the account of your stewardship; show how you heard the commandments, how you dealt with fellow-slaves, either kindly and philanthropically or, on the contrary, greedily and tyrannically, striking, beating, and depriving them of the grain-measure of alms.'

If he is able to make the master appeased by proving himself a good servant, it would be well for him; but if on the contrary, there are no longer whips and rods there, nor dark mills and iron pedals, but unquenchable fire and eternal darkness never illuminated by light, and the gnashing of teeth, which the gospel has clearly revealed to us (Matt 25:30).

Therefore, if he never casts out from here as if they were strangers, let him waste the world and let pleasure remain unhindered according to every sense. But if these things will be accomplished, even if we do not enjoy them for long, let us fear, brothers, the transfer from this place, and let us live in the time of sojourning as the Lord commanded; let us not be carried away as debtors, but let us walk free, being led by a good conscience, carrying the books of the life's citizenship unsearchably.

That rich man was a bad steward of this life, whose land was fruitful, because regarding the abundance of fruits, man did not counsel anything good, but opening the desire of the stomach and the wide and insatiable bellies of greed, he allotted everything to his own enjoyment, saying, 'I will pull down my barns and build greater, and I will say to my soul: You have many good things laid up, rest, eat, drink, rejoice' (Luke 12:19-20). And while he was speaking, the one taking him arrived. A terrible fellow-slave came to snatch him away from the stewardship; and what is the profit of a love-of-money plan?

And these things were written vividly for our instruction. But what is the experience of life? Not every single day do these things cry out through works; I showed us the one healthy in the middle of the day becoming dead before the onset of evening; and the one strengthening himself in the evening, not grasping the morning ray; and another perishing in the midst of eating and living. Who then is so foolish, as not to realize that every day another [comes] of this [place]...

Are we being moved from our stewardship? But the good and faithful steward, having trusted in his own management, has a will such as Paul had. For he, when the Lord was not hurrying, hastened to him and desired the dismissal and was willing to relinquish the stewardship, saying in one way: 'Wretched am I a man, who will rescue me from this body of death?' (Rom 7:24) and again: 'For to me it is good to be dissolved and to be with Christ' (Phil 1:23). But the earthly man, whose mindset is truly kin to the oxen, laments such things helplessly at the transition, like this man in the parable: 'What shall I do, since my lord is taking the stewardship from me? I am not able to dig, and I am ashamed to beg' (Luke 16:3).

His grief is that of the idle and the lover of pleasure. For to wail at the departure is a reproach of having been added to the estate and of lamenting the passionate enjoyments of the flesh, while the inability toward the work of an idle life and a fallen state is an accusation. For if he had had a habit of love for labor, he would not have feared digging.

If we take the parable allegorically toward the spiritual, after this transition, there is neither working nor having time for increase. And because of this, let no one say: 'I am not able to dig.'
